opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that the workload has shifted. A few years ago, most of the compute went into training. You trained a model once, and inference was kind of an afterthought. Now these models are deployed to hundreds of millions of people. And with reasoning models and agents, the model generates thousands or tens of thousands of tokens before it even gives you an answer. So inference is where most of the compute, and most of the cost, ends up going.

If that's true, then when you design an architecture you should be asking: how efficient is this at generation time? The constraints there are different from training. Training is very parallel, so you can saturate the tensor cores, and you're mostly compute-bound. Decoding is sequential. You generate one token at a time, and you're often bottlenecked by memory bandwidth. You have to load the model weights and the KV cache for every token. As context gets longer and you have more concurrent users, the KV cache becomes the dominant cost.

That's part of the motivation for things like state space models, Mamba, and these hybrid architectures. They keep a fixed-size state instead of a cache that grows with sequence length. It's also why people are looking at multi-query attention, grouped-query attention, latent attention like what DeepSeek did, and lower precision. These are all ways of reducing the memory you have to move per token.

There's also a hardware angle. You want arithmetic intensity, meaning enough compute per byte you load so that you actually use the GPU. A lot of my work has been about co-designing the algorithm with the hardware. An architecture can look great on paper in FLOPs and still be slow in practice if it doesn't map well to how the hardware moves data.

So inference-first doesn't mean ignoring quality. The model still has to be good. But if two architectures are roughly comparable in quality and one is two or three times cheaper to serve, that matters a lot. It means you can serve more users, use longer contexts, or let the model think longer for the same budget. And letting models think longer is increasingly how we get better answers. So inference efficiency turns into capability.

r001.rationale: The response mentions Mamba and hybrid architectures as ways to reduce inference memory costs, but does not identify hybrid Transformer–Mamba architectures or clearly connect that combination to a quality–efficiency tradeoff.

r002.rationale: The response says inference is where most of the compute ends up going, which communicates that most model FLOPs are spent on inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that inference is where the model actually lives. Training happens once, or a handful of times, but every token anyone ever gets out of the model goes through inference, and that cost compounds forever. So if you only optimize for training throughput, you can end up with an architecture that was cheap to build and expensive to use, and that's exactly backwards given how these things get deployed.

The deeper reason is that the bottlenecks are different. Training is mostly compute-bound. You have big batches, you're doing large matrix multiplies, the GPU is happy. Inference, especially decoding, is memory-bound. You're generating one token at a time, you have to read the entire KV cache for every step, and the arithmetic intensity is terrible. So the question that matters shifts from "how many FLOPs does this layer cost" to "how many bytes do I have to move per token, and how much state do I have to carry around." That's a very different design pressure, and attention as originally formulated is not kind to it. The KV cache grows linearly with context, and at long context it's the dominant cost.

That's really what motivated the state-space and linear-attention work, Mamba and the hybrids. If you have a fixed-size recurrent state, decoding cost is constant per token regardless of how long the context is. You give up a bit of precise recall compared to full attention, but it turns out you can mix a small number of attention layers with mostly SSM layers and keep most of the quality while making inference dramatically cheaper. You wouldn't have arrived at that design if you were just staring at training loss curves.

It also forces you to think about the hardware honestly. FlashAttention came out of the same mindset: the algorithm was fine, the memory traffic was the problem. Once you internalize that the memory hierarchy is the real constraint, you start asking at the architecture level, not just the kernel level, what shape of model makes the hardware happy at serving time. Batch size, context length, how much you can parallelize across requests, whether the thing fits in one GPU's HBM. Those are architectural questions as much as systems questions.

And practically, inference efficiency is what unlocks capability now. Reasoning models generate thousands of tokens of chain of thought. Agents run long loops. Test-time compute only pays off if each token is cheap. So designing for inference isn't just a cost-saving exercise anymore, it's what determines what you can afford to let the model do.

r001.rationale: It describes combining a small number of attention layers with mostly SSM layers to retain most model quality while making inference much cheaper, and identifies Mamba among this work.

r002.rationale: It says inference costs compound across generated tokens, but does not state that inference accounts for most of the FLOPs spent on models.

astra-6.text:
Because inference is where you pay the cost over and over again. You train a model once—or a few times—but you might serve it to millions of users. So I like to start with the constraints you’ll face when you actually use it: how quickly can it respond, how much memory does it need, and how many requests can you serve?

Those questions affect the architecture. With a Transformer, for example, the KV cache grows with context length, and that can become expensive during generation. That motivates looking at architectures that can keep a fixed-size state, or hybrids that combine that property with attention.

Of course, the model still has to be good. The goal is to work backward from an efficient inference design and ask: can we train this effectively, and can we get the quality we need? I think that’s a productive way to guide architecture research.

sol-6.1.text:
I favor inference-first design because training is a cost you pay up front, while inference is a cost you keep paying every time someone uses the model. So I like to start with the question: what would make this model efficient to serve? Then we can work backward and figure out how to train it well.

That changes which architectural properties you care about. With a Transformer, for example, the KV cache grows with the context length, and during generation you have to keep reading that information from memory. An architecture that compresses the history into a fixed-size state has a different efficiency profile, especially for long sequences.

Of course, efficiency alone isn't enough. You still need quality, and you need a model that trains effectively on the hardware you have. But I think inference should be a constraint you design around from the beginning, because it's much harder to fix an expensive architecture after you've trained it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Transformer KV caches and fixed-size state architectures, but does not identify a hybrid Transformer–Mamba architecture or say it improves the quality–inference-efficiency tradeoff.
